source_claims.statement: C++ originated as an extension of C and evolved into a multi-paradigm language.
Stroustrup began C with Classes at Bell Labs in 1979.
C++ combines direct hardware mapping with zero-overhead abstractions.
C++ is standardized by ISO WG21 and has successive revisions.
The standard library spans containers, iterators, ranges, algorithms, numerics, I/O, memory, metaprogramming, diagnostics and concurrency.
The STL model of containers, iterators and generic algorithms became part of the standard library.
C++ is not strictly a superset of C.
extern C enables C linkage for mixed C/C++ functions.
Assembly integration varies by compiler and architecture.
Core Guidelines target type/resource safety but are not ISO consensus.
Manual memory misuse can introduce security risks such as buffer overflow.
C++ influenced a broad set of later languages.

references_resources.label: The Design and Evolution of C++

semantic_distinctions.explanation: C++ shares most C syntax but is not a strict superset.
C++ is the standardized language; GCC/Clang/MSVC/etc. are implementations.
ISO defines the language/library; Core Guidelines are external guidance.
Headers are traditional inclusion; modules provide importable/named mechanisms.
Inline is compiler-specific embedded assembly; standalone is separate and linked.
Source is program text; object code is compiled binary output.
Similar source does not guarantee binary compatibility across compilers.
Templates provide generic programming; virtual functions provide dynamic dispatch.
extern C selects C linkage for interoperating functions.
STL's core generic model is part of a larger standard library.
Manual memory is a capability whose misuse can create risks.
C++23/C++26 are language revisions, not compiler names.

learning_paths.title: ABI
learning_paths.sequence: name mangling → exception ABI → binary compatibility

misconceptions.claim: C++ is just C with classes
misconceptions.correction: It expanded into generic, functional, object-oriented, modular and other capabilities.

misconceptions.claim: C++ is a strict superset of C
STL is the whole standard library
misconceptions.correction: STL's model became part of a larger standard library.
Templates are a general generic-programming mechanism.

misconceptions.claim: All C++ compilers have compatible object code
misconceptions.correction: ABI implementation choices can make object code incompatible.
Its syntax and availability vary by compiler and architecture.

misconceptions.claim: Core Guidelines are the ISO standard
misconceptions.correction: The source says they are not ISO consensus.
The source says misuse can introduce risks; manual control is a capability.
Zero-overhead abstractions are a central design goal.

misconceptions.claim: C and C++ can always be mixed directly
misconceptions.correction: Cross-boundary functions may require C linkage.
